raw_text:
Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is a progressive, infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils within the myocardial interstitium [1]. Historically considered a rare, untreatable condition, CA is now recognized as an underdiagnosed cause of heart failure (HF), particularly heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) [2]. The two primary amyloid proteins responsible for over 95% of clinical cases are immunoglobulin light chain (AL) and transthyretin (ATTR) [3].

### Pathophysiology
AL amyloidosis arises from a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia producing toxic monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains that deposit in various organs, including the heart [4]. It represents a medical emergency due to its rapid progression and direct cardiotoxicity [5]. Conversely, ATTR amyloidosis results from the dissociation of the transthyretin homotetramer, synthesized primarily by the liver, into unstable monomers that misfold and aggregate [6]. ATTR occurs in two forms: wild-type ATTR (ATTRwt), predominantly affecting older males, and hereditary ATTR (ATTRv), caused by autosomal dominant pathogenic variants in the *TTR* gene (most commonly Val122Ile, Val30Met, and Thr60Ala) [7, 8].

### Clinical Manifestations
The clinical presentation of CA is characterized by restrictive cardiomyopathy leading to progressive biventricular heart failure, arrhythmias, and conduction blocks [9]. Systemic red flags often predate cardiac symptoms, particularly in ATTR. These include bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, biceps tendon rupture, and autonomic dysfunction [10, 11].

### Diagnostic Advances
Early diagnosis is critical but historically delayed. Electrocardiography (ECG) may show low voltage or a pseudoinfarction pattern, but the classic discordance between low ECG voltage and marked left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) on echocardiography is highly suggestive [12]. Echocardiographic hallmarks include concentric LV wall thickening, biatrial enlargement, and a restrictive filling pattern. Tissue Doppler imaging reveals decreased longitudinal strain with characteristic "apical sparing" [13, 14].

Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging provides exquisite tissue characterization. Standard features include diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement (LGE), elevated native T1 relaxation times, and increased extracellular volume (ECV) fraction [15, 16, 17].

A major paradigm shift occurred with the validation of non-invasive diagnostic algorithms. Technetium-labeled bone-scintigraphy (using $^{99\text{m}}\text{Tc}$-pyrophosphate [PYP], $^{99\text{m}}\text{Tc}$-3,3-diphono-1,2-propanodicarboxylic acid [DPD], or $^{99\text{m}}\text{Tc}$-hydroxymethylene diphosphonate [HMDP]) shows intense myocardial uptake (Grade 2 or 3) in ATTR patients [18, 19]. Crucially, a non-invasive diagnosis of ATTR can only be established in the absolute absence of a monoclonal protein. Therefore, screening with serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis (IFE) and serum free light chain (FLC) assays is mandatory [20, 21]. If a monoclonal protein is detected, or if non-invasive results are equivocal, an endomyocardial biopsy remains the gold standard, requiring Congo red staining demonstrating apple-green birefringence under polarized light, followed by mass spectrometry or immunohistochemistry [22, 23, 24].

### Therapeutic Landscape
Treatment of AL amyloidosis targets the underlying plasma cell clone. The current standard of care for newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis includes the combination of the anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody daratumumab with bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone (Dara-CyBorD), which has significantly improved hematologic and cardiac response rates [25]. Autologous stem cell transplantation remains an option for eligible patients [26].

For ATTR amyloidosis, therapeutic strategies are categorized into TTR stabilization and TTR gene silencing. Tafamidis, an oral small-molecule TTR stabilizer, was shown in the landmark ATTR-ACT trial to significantly reduce all-cause mortality and cardiovascular-related hospitalizations in both ATTRwt and ATTRv patients [27]. More recently, gene-silencing therapeutics that degrade TTR messenger RNA have emerged. Patisiran and inotersen halt TTR production in the liver [28, 29]. While initially approved for hereditary ATTR polyneuropathy, clinical trials have demonstrated their efficacy in improving cardiac parameters, functional capacity, and quality of life in patients with ATTR cardiomyopathy [30].

### Conclusion
The management of cardiac amyloidosis has undergone a major revolution. Transitioning from a disease diagnosed post-mortem to one that can be diagnosed non-invasively and managed with disease-modifying therapies, CA now demands heightened clinical suspicion and early multidisciplinary intervention to optimize patient outcomes.
